docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This datasheet provides a complete overview of the Sensor Subsystem Board used in the Smart Irrigation System project. The subsystem is designed to measure soil moisture levels and send that data to the main control unit in turn helping the system make decisions about when to water.

The document outlines how the subsystem works, what components were selected, and how power is managed to ensure reliable performance. It includes the block diagram, component selections, bill of materials (BOM), schematic, power budget, and appendix for full reference listed above.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
The Smart Irrigation System is a water-efficient lawn watering project designed by Team 101. Its goal is to help homeowners and renters maintain healthy lawns while reducing water waste and cost. The system automatically monitors soil conditions, weather, and water usage to decide when watering is needed.

The project is built around three main subsystems — Control, Sensor, and Motor — each using a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller. These subsystems work together to create a modular and reliable watering system that can function both online and offline.

My subsystem, the Sensor Board, plays a key role by measuring soil moisture levels and sending accurate data to the Control Board. This data allows the system to decide when to turn the pump on or off, helping achieve efficient and automatic lawn irrigation.

For a full overview of the team project, including our mission statement, user needs, and system design, you can visit the Team Report Appendix.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My part in this project focuses on the Sensor Subsystem, which handles data collection and signal processing for the soil moisture readings. I designed the board to convert a 9V supply down to 5V using an LM7805 regulator and included diode and fuse protection for safe operation. The board uses an MCP6004 op-amp to condition the sensor signal before it’s read by the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

The processed data is then sent to the Control Subsystem through an 8-pin connector to support system coordination. My design ensures that the sensor data is clean, stable, and accurate, which is essential for the irrigation logic to function properly.

To review the materials and components used to build this subsystem, visit the BOM section of this datasheet. For information on circuit layout and wiring, see the Schematic section. For power usage and regulation details, check the Power Budget section.

This subsystem provides the foundation for the system’s “decision-making,” ensuring the smart irrigation setup reacts correctly to real soil conditions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This subsystem monitors soil saturation levels using an analog soil moisture sensor. A Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller reads the sensor’s analog output, processes the data, and transmits the results to the main system for further analysis and control actions.

Power is supplied by a 9V, 3A wall adapter, which is regulated down to 5V, 1.5A through a voltage regulator to provide stable and safe operation for both the microcontroller and sensor.

docs.title: Sensors and Interfaces
docs.text:
Connected Sensor: Analog Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor

System Interface: Communicates soil data to other subsystems (e.g., motor control or irrigation logic) through an 8-pin connector, enabling coordinated system responses based on soil conditions.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: Subsystem board powered from 9 V input through a 5 V regulator. Includes a PIC18F16Q41 Curiosity Nano microcontroller connected to: - Analog soil moisture sensor - Temperature / humidity sensor - Rain sensor - 8-pin connector to communicate with other boards

docs.title: Soil Moisture Sensors
docs.text:
Table 1: Soil Moisture Sensor Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: SEN0114 Soil Moisture Sensor Module$2.70 — eachlink to product Simple analog outputLow costCompact design Corrodes over time if left in soilRequires calibration for accuracy Option 2: ST0160 Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor V2.0$8.60 — eachlink to product No corrosion (capacitive)Stable analog readingsLow power consumption More expensive than SEN0114Slightly larger PCB footprint Option 3: Industrial Soil Moisture & Temperature Sensor$79 — eachlink to product Industrial-grade durabilityIncludes temperature outputLong-term outdoor reliability Higher costRequires analog-to-current interface circuitry

Choice: Option 2 — ST0160 Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor V2.0

Rationale: Provides much more corrosion-free sensing with stable analog output and is good for long-term moisture monitoring in outdoor environments while maintaining low cost and simple integration with the PIC ADC.

docs.title: Temperature & Humidity Sensors
docs.text:
Table 2: Temperature & Humidity Sensor Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: DHT22 / AM2302 Sensor$9.39 — eachlink to product Low costSimple one-wire interfaceGood community support Slow sampling rateLimited accuracy (±0.5 °C, ±2 % RH) Option 2: Adafruit Sensirion SHT31-D Sensor (I²C)$13.95 — eachlink to product High accuracy (±0.3 °C, ±2 % RH)I²C communicationFast response time Moderate costRequires I²C pins on MCU Option 3: SHT45 Precision Temperature Humidity Module$14.99 — eachlink to product Very high precision (±0.1 °C, ±1 % RH)Low power consumptionCompact form factor Higher priceMay require fine-pitch connector or adapter

Choice: Option 2 — Adafruit Sensirion SHT31-D Sensor

Rationale: Offers a balance between precision, power efficiency, and integration simplicity using I²C communication working well with the PIC18F16Q41’s peripheral support.

docs.title: Rain Water Sensors
docs.text:
Table 3: Rain Sensor Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: ST0247 Raindrop Detection Sensor Module$8.60 — eachlink to product Low cost and easy to interfaceAnalog and digital outputs Susceptible to corrosion and false positivesNot quantitative Option 2: SEN0545 Rain Sensor (UART Output)$22.68 — eachlink to product Digital UART interfaceCorrosion-resistant coatingStable signal processing built-in Slightly higher costRequires UART parsing logic Option 3: Optical Rain Gauge Sensor (RS485 Pulse Output)$85.72 — eachlink to product Industrial precision and long lifetimeNon-contact optical detection High priceRequires RS485 interface and external housing

Choice: Option 2 — SEN0545 Rain Sensor (UART Output)

Rationale: Provides reliable digital output with minimal maintenance and better environmental resistance than basic analog boards and avoiding the complexity and cost of industrial RS485 systems.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
Table 4: Voltage Regulator Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: LM7805 Linear Regulator$0.64 — eachlink to product Simple designLow noiseStable 5 V output Inefficient when dropping 9 V to 5 VGenerates heat at higher currents Option 2: UA78L05ACLP $1.69 — eachlink to product Compact packageLow quiescent currentPerfect for ≤ 100 mA loads Limited output current (100 mA max)Not ideal for high-current systems

Choice: Option 1 — LM7805 Linear Regulator

Rationale: System current is moderate so the LM7805 offers sufficient efficiency with low noise, needed for stable analog measurements on the sensor inputs.

docs.title: Microcontroller
docs.text:
Component: PIC18F16Q41 Curiosity Nano Supply: 5 V from LM7805 Regulator

Rationale: Used for its low-power operation, built-in ADC channels for analog sensor inputs, I²C and UART support for digital sensors, and fast development and debugging.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This schematic is designed to support the Smart Irrigation Subsystem Board. It regulates a DC 9V wall adapter input down to 5 V using an LM7805 linear regulator with diode and fuse protection. The 5 V rail powers a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller that monitors capacitive soil moisture ST0160 using an MCP6004 op-amp to amplify/filter the signal. The system provides stable sensor inputs, onboard filtering, and a ribbon connector for inter-board communication.”

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text:
Team Number: 101 Project Name: Smart Irrigation Sensor Subsystem Board Team Member Names: Liam, Isaiah, Myles, and Raj Version: 1.3

System input: 9V external → 5V regulator (LM7805) → PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano + Soil Moisture Sensor + MCP6004 Op-Amp

docs.title: Section A – All Major Components
docs.text:
Component Name Part / Example Supply Voltage (V) Qty. Abs. Max Current (mA) Total Current (mA) Microcontroller (Curiosity Nano) PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano 5 1 500 500 Soil Moisture Sensor ST0160 Capacitive 5 1 5 5 Operational Amplifier MCP6004 (Quad Op-Amp, TH) 5 1 23 23 Subtotal 528 mA

Arithmetic (component sum): 500 + 5 + 23 = 528 mA total subsystem current

docs.title: Section B – Power Rails
docs.text:
+5V Rail - Subtotal = 528 mA - Safety margin (25%) = 528 × 1.25 = 660 mA

Arithmetic (with margin): 528 × 1.25 = (528 × 5) / 4 = 2640 / 4 = 660.0 mA

Rounded total (for spec/selection): 660 mA

docs.title: Section C – Regulator Selection
docs.text:
Regulator Option Input Range (V) Max Output (mA) Pros Cons LM7805 (linear) 7 – 25V 1500 Simple, low noise, reliable Inefficient (9V→5V drop causes heat; needs heat sink) UA78L05ACLP (TO-92, 100 mA max) 7 – 35V 100 Compact, low quiescent current Not enough output current for system needs

Choice: LM7805 Linear Regulator

Rationale: With a total estimated current requirement of 660 mA (including margin), an LM7805 (1.5 A rated in common packages or variants) provides ample output capacity and thermal design margin. The UA78L05ACLP (100 mA) is insufficient.

Regulator heat / dissipation check: - Voltage drop = 9 V − 5 V = 4 V - Load current (with margin) = 660 mA = 0.660 A - Power dissipated = 4 V × 0.660 A = 2.64 W

Result: The LM7805 will require a small heat sink for continuous operation at this load.

docs.title: Section D – External Power Source
docs.text:
Power Source Example Output Voltage (V) Max Current (mA) Wall Adapter Generic 9V DC Adapter 9 3000
  • Required on +5V rail (with 25% margin): 660 mA
  • Remaining capacity on 9V, 3A adapter: 3000 − 660 = 2340 mA

Arithmetic: 3000 − 660 = 2340 mA remaining

Battery Option (not implemented): If powered by a 3000 mAh battery (for estimation only):

  • Example sleep-mode average current = 50 mA → battery life = 3000 mAh / 50 mA = 60 hours (≈ 2.5 days)
  • With active current near the full draw (528 mA), battery life = 3000 / 528 ≈ 5.68 hours (not practical for continuous operation)

docs.title: Section E – Summary
docs.text:
Item Value / Action Subtotal (estimated) 528 mA Total required on 5V rail (with 25% margin) 660 mA Regulator chosen LM7805 Linear Regulator Regulator dissipation (9→5V at 660 mA) ≈ 2.64 W (heat sink required) External supply recommended 9V DC adapter, ≥ 3 A Estimated battery life (3000 mAh Li-ion) ≈ 60 hours (sleep-mode avg) / ≈ 5.7 hours (continuous active draw)

Conclusion: After including the MCP6004 (23 mA max), the subsystem’s estimated current draw is 528 mA. With a 25% safety margin the design calls for 660 mA on the 5V rail. The chosen LM7805 regulator will need a small heat sink to safely dissipate about 2.64 W when powered from the 9V adapter. The 9V, 3A wall adapter provides ample headroom (≈ 2.34 A spare capacity).
